transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Well, I came because... it’s my husband’s sister. She has been working this family business, just scheming so she can get control of the money and push me right out of all the decisions. And no matter how folks try to smooth it over, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. It’s clear as day. 

Just like... well, speaking of a year, last year around this time we had that awful freeze. Do you remember that? It completely wiped out my garden. I had these big, beautiful beefsteak tomatoes growing, and I even told my neighbor she better cover hers up with a tarp or she'd lose them all. I always get my tarps from that little hardware store off Route 9, but they shut down recently. It’s a real shame, too, because the new place that opened up in town just doesn't carry the heavy-duty ones, and their parking lot is always such a mess with all the potholes. You can barely get a cart through there without twisting an ankle. 

Anyway, I just... I needed to tell someone what's going on with her.
Do you believe for certain that your husband’s sister is deliberately trying to take control of the money and push you out?

Well, yes, like I was just saying, I am one hundred percent certain. I've been watching her for over a year now, and no matter how much folks try to smooth it over and make excuses for her, I know she's trying to grab the money and push me out of all the decisions with the business. 

Money just... well, it makes people act so ugly. Speaking of money, I went down to the bank on Tuesday to cash a small check, and you know that teller, the one with the bright red glasses? Well, she had this new haircut, just all chopped up in the back. I don't know why anyone would pay good money for a haircut like that. My cousin Tammy went to cosmetology school back in the nineties, down in... oh, what was the name of that town? It was right past the county line, had that big water tower. Anyway, Tammy always said if you don't layer it right, you end up looking like a wet poodle. And that's exactly what this teller looked like. I almost offered her a hat, it was that bad. She took forever counting my bills, too. 

But, um... what was I saying? Oh, right, my husband's sister. Yes, I'm certain about what she's doing.
Do you ever hear voices when no one else is there?

Voices? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. Just regular folks talking. But speaking of hearing things, I was sitting on my porch yesterday evening, and the neighbor's dog—that little scruffy terrier mix they got from the pound—would not stop barking. Just yapping and yapping at every car that went by. They let him out on a long chain, and he gets tangled around the old oak tree in their front yard. I told my husband, I said, 'If they don't untangle that poor dog, he's gonna choke himself.' 

My husband, he just tunes it out. He can sit in his recliner with the television blaring, watching those old Westerns. You know, the ones in black and white where they always have a shootout at high noon? He loves those. We had to buy a new antenna for the TV last month because the wind blew the old one right off the roof. The guy who came to fix it was so young, he looked like he should still be in high school. I offered him some lemonade, but he said he was in a hurry to get to his next job over in Shelbyville. 

But no, to answer your question, I don't hear any voices that aren't there. Just the dog and the TV, mostly.
Has your husband’s sister done anything that would be impossible for most people, like controlling your thoughts or sending you special messages?

Controlling my thoughts? Lord, no. She's not a witch or anything, she can't do things like that. No special messages either. 

Though, speaking of messages, our mail carrier—Gary, I think his name is, he wears those little blue shorts even when it's freezing out—he keeps leaving the neighbor's mail in my box. Just yesterday I got a whole stack of those glossy catalogs meant for the folks two doors down. One of them was for that fancy outdoor furniture, you know the kind with the thick cushions that cost an arm and a leg? I always say, why pay that much when the squirrels are just gonna chew right through them anyway. We had a squirrel get onto our back porch last spring, just tore the stuffing right out of the seat on my favorite rocking chair. My husband tried to patch it up with silver duct tape, which looks just awful. I told him we should go down to the flea market on Sunday and see if we can find a replacement cushion, but he hates the traffic over by the fairgrounds. It does get backed up all the way to the highway when they have the antique shows. 

But, um, what were you asking me? Oh, right, his sister. No, she can't control my mind or do anything impossible. She's just a regular, sneaky person trying to get her hands on the business money, that's all.
Have you had a period when your mood was unusually high or irritable for days at a time?

Unusually high? Or irritable? No, I wouldn't say that. I'm pretty even-keeled, mostly. I mean, everybody gets a little cranky now and then, but not for days on end. 

Now, if you want to talk about irritable, you should see my husband when his truck won't start. He's got this old Ford, 1998 I think, maroon color, but the clear coat is peeling off the hood so bad it looks like the poor thing has a terrible sunburn. He just refuses to get it painted. We took it down to the mechanic a few weeks ago... Sal, I think his name is? He's got that big garage over on Elm, right next to the diner. His shop always smells like old French fries because of the exhaust fan from the kitchen next door blowing right into his open bays. 

That diner used to have the absolute best cherry pie, but they changed owners last fall. The new guy brought in all these fancy menus with those thick plastic covers, and they always stick together when it's humid out. I just can't stand that. You try to open it up to look at the breakfast specials and it makes this awful ripping sound, like you're tearing the whole thing apart. And they stopped serving the cherry pie, too. Replaced it with some kind of lemon tart that's just way too sour. I told the waitress, I said, 'Nobody wants a sour dessert after a heavy meal,' but she just smiled and gave me the check. 

But, um... wait, what was the question again? My mood? Right, right. No, I don't get high or irritable like that. I'm just my regular self.
Do people ever tell you that your speech is hard to follow or that you go off track when you talk?

Hard to follow? Off track? Well, I suppose sometimes my husband says I talk too much, but he's not one to talk. He barely says two words most days unless it's about his garden. 

He planted these Big Boy tomatoes this year, right along the back fence where the sun hits best in the afternoon. But you know, the deer keep getting into them. They just hop right over the chain-link like it's nothing. I told him we need to put up some of that chicken wire, maybe string up some shiny pie tins to scare them off. My grandmother used to do that. She had this huge garden out behind her farmhouse, and she'd hang these old aluminum pie plates from the branches of her peach trees. They'd clatter together in the wind and make this awful racket. It worked, though. We used to sit out on her wraparound porch and pit peaches all afternoon for canning. She made the best peach preserves, used real cane sugar and a little pinch of nutmeg. I tried making it once, but I scorched the bottom of the pan and it took me three days of soaking to get the burnt sugar off. I ended up having to use baking soda and a wire brush, and it scratched the enamel right off my favorite Dutch oven. 

Anyway... what were you saying? Oh, my speech. No, nobody really tells me I'm hard to follow. I just like to explain things properly, you know?
Aside from the conflict with your husband’s sister, have you been having trouble managing your usual day-to-day activities?

Trouble managing my day-to-day? Oh, no, I'm doing just fine with all that. I still keep up with my quilting group on Tuesdays, and choir practice on Thursday nights. We're actually learning this beautiful new arrangement of "Amazing Grace" right now. Our choir director, Mr. Henderson, he's got this booming baritone voice, but he's so particular about the sopranos hitting their high notes. He makes us do these silly warm-up exercises where we have to buzz our lips like a horse. It looks absolutely ridiculous, let me tell you. Mrs. Gable, she sits next to me in the alto section, and she always wears this bright red lipstick that ends up smeared all over her chin by the time we're done warming up. I keep telling her she ought to switch to one of those long-lasting stains, you know, the kind you have to scrub off with cold cream. I bought a tube of it at the pharmacy last week—the one over on Main Street, not the big chain store out by the highway. The pharmacist there, Dave, he always gives me a little discount on my vitamins. He's got a son who just started high school, playing trumpet in the marching band. They had their first game on Friday, and it rained cats and dogs. Those poor kids in their wool uniforms must have smelled like wet dogs by the end of the night. 

Oh, and I'm still doing my GED lessons, and my senior walks at the mall on Monday mornings. So, no, my daily stuff is fine. Mostly, this whole thing with his sister has just changed how much I trust her, you know? And it definitely makes me think twice about which family gatherings I feel comfortable going to. I skipped the Labor Day barbecue entirely because I just couldn't stomach the thought of her being there.
Has anyone been able to convince you that you might be mistaken about your husband’s sister?

Mistaken? Oh, no. People try to smooth it over, sure. They say, "Oh, she's just being helpful," or "She's just trying to pitch in." But I came because my husband’s sister has been working this family business so she can get control of all the money and push me right out of any decisions. And no matter what folks say, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. 

It's just like when my cousin Larry tried to take over my uncle's hardware store. Larry was always a smooth talker, you know? He'd come in with these big boxes of donuts from that bakery downtown—the one with the pink awning that got blown off in the storm last spring. They never did replace that awning, just left the metal frame sitting there looking like an old skeleton. Anyway, Larry would bring these donuts, the glazed ones with the little sprinkles, and sit in the back office acting like he owned the place. He started ordering all this inventory nobody wanted, like those electric snow shovels. Who buys an electric snow shovel? You just end up dragging a cord through the wet snow, and then you trip over it and break your hip. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she broke her hip two winters ago slipping on the ice by her mailbox. She was in rehab for months, and when she came back, she had to use one of those walkers with the tennis balls on the feet. I always wondered who came up with that idea, putting tennis balls on walkers. It seems so silly, but I guess it stops them from scuffing up the linoleum. 

But, what was I... oh, right. No, I'm not mistaken. She's trying to push me out, and nobody can convince me otherwise. I see right through her.
Before all this with your husband’s sister, have you generally found it hard to trust other people?

Hard to trust people? No, not really. I've always been a pretty trusting person, you know? I mean, I try to see the good in folks. Like my neighbor down the street, Mr. Abernathy. 

He moved in about three years ago, right after his wife passed away. She had a bad heart, I think. Anyway, he started leaving these little baskets of vegetables from his garden on my front porch. Just out of the blue! Zucchini, mostly. You know how zucchini is, once it starts growing, you can't stop it. You have to practically give it away to strangers on the street. I made so much zucchini bread that summer, I thought my husband was going to turn green. I use my mother's recipe, the one with the walnuts and a little bit of cinnamon. But walnuts are getting so expensive these days. I was at the grocery store last week—the one with the new self-checkout lanes that never seem to work right—and a little bag of walnuts was almost eight dollars! Can you believe that? The cashier, a sweet young girl named Chloe, she said it's because of a drought somewhere out west. She's saving up for college, wants to study marine biology. I always thought that sounded so interesting, working with dolphins and whales. I saw a documentary once about these whales that sing to each other across the ocean. It's so beautiful, but a little sad, too, don't you think? Just calling out into the dark water, hoping someone hears you. 

But, um... what were we talking about? Oh, trusting people. No, before this whole mess with her, I never really had a problem trusting people. I just take them as they come.
What exactly has your husband’s sister done that makes you believe she is trying to take control of the money and push you out?

Well, it's just... it's the way she acts, you know? She's always hovering around the business accounts, always asking these little questions about where the money's going. And she started bringing in these fancy new ledger books. I don't know what was wrong with the old ones, the green ones with the gold lettering on the front. We used to buy them at that stationery shop downtown, the one next to the old movie theater. 

They tore that theater down last year, you know. It was a shame, really. I saw my first movie there, "The Sound of Music." My mother took me, and we sat right in the middle row. The seats were covered in this red velvet that was practically worn bald on the armrests. And they had the best popcorn. They used real butter, not that yellow oil stuff they squirt on it now. My husband loves popcorn, but he always burns it in the microwave. He sets the timer for three minutes and then walks away to watch the news. The news is just so depressing lately, isn't it? All these storms and things. My sister-in-law in Florida—not the one I'm talking about, my brother's wife—she had to evacuate twice last year because of hurricanes. She packed up her two cats and drove all the way up to Georgia. The cats hated it, of course. One of them, a big orange tabby named Marmalade, yowled the entire six hours. I had an orange cat once, when I was a little girl... 

But I'm sorry, what did you ask me? What exactly did she do? Well, I don't know exactly, it's just... I just know she's trying to push me out. You can just tell with some people, can't you?
Is it possible that you could be wrong about your husband’s sister?

Wrong? No, no, I couldn't be wrong. Like I said before, I came here because my husband's sister has been working this family business just so she can get control of the money and push me out of all the decisions. People try to smooth it over, tell me I'm imagining things, but no matter what folks try to say, I know what I've been seeing for more than a year now. 

It's just like when you see a storm rolling in. You know it's coming. The sky gets that weird greenish-purple color, like a bruised plum. My grandmother used to make the best plum preserves. She had this big copper pot she'd stir them in, and she'd stand over the stove for hours with this long wooden spoon. The spoon was stained dark purple at the end. She always said the secret was a pinch of nutmeg, but I think it was just the amount of sugar she used. She kept her sugar in this old tin canister that had a picture of a windmill on it. I always liked that windmill. I wanted to visit Holland when I was younger, to see the tulips and the windmills. I saw a picture in a magazine once of a whole field of red and yellow tulips. It looked like a quilt spread out over the ground. My aunt made me a quilt for my wedding, actually. It was a double wedding ring pattern, all done in blues and whites. But the dog we had then—a little terrier mix named Buster—he chewed a hole right through the corner of it. He was a good dog, though, just a little anxious during thunderstorms... 

But anyway, no, I'm not wrong about her. I've been watching her for a year, and I know exactly what she's trying to do with the business and the money. I see it plain as day.
Has your husband's sister done anything that would be impossible in real life?

Impossible? Like magic or something? No, she hasn't done anything like that. She's just sneaky, you know? Just... regular sneaky. Although, I swear sometimes it feels like she can read my mind, the way she knows exactly when I'm going to check the mail so she can get to the bank statements first. Our mail carrier, Gary, he's been doing this route for twenty years. He walks with a little bit of a limp now because he slipped on the ice on Mrs. Higgins' driveway two winters ago. She never shovels her walk, Mrs. Higgins. She just throws down this cheap rock salt that ruins the concrete. It eats right through it, leaves these little pockmarks everywhere. My husband tried to tell her once, but she just waved him off. She's practically deaf in one ear, anyway. She used to play the French horn in the symphony orchestra, back in the sixties. I can't imagine carrying one of those big brass things around, they look so heavy and complicated. All those valves and tubes. My nephew played the trumpet in middle school, but he gave it up because it made his lips swell up...

Wait, what did you ask me? Impossible things? No, no, nothing impossible. Just... very underhanded.
What specific evidence do you have that makes you sure your husband’s sister is trying to take control of the money?

Evidence? Well, I don't... I don't have, like, a piece of paper or a recording or anything like that. It's just... I just know it. It's the way she looks at the ledgers, the way she asks about the accounts. You don't need a photograph to know someone's sneaking around behind your back. 

My mother used to say that, actually. She'd say, "You don't need a weatherman to know which way the wind blows." She loved that song, the Bob Dylan one. We had it on an old 45 record. The label was yellow and orange, I think. We kept all the records in this wooden crate in the living room, right next to the console television. That TV was a piece of furniture, I tell you. It had these big wooden doors you could close over the screen when you weren't watching it. Not like these flat things people hang on the wall now. They just look like black mirrors when they're turned off. I don't like them. They reflect everything in the room. I saw myself in one at the appliance store the other day and I thought, "Lord, when did I get so gray?" My hairdresser, Patty, she says she can put a rinse in it, but I don't know. Those chemicals smell so strong. They remind me of the pool at the YMCA where my kids took swimming lessons. The chlorine was so thick you could taste it in the air. My youngest, he hated getting his face wet. He'd wear these little goggles that left red rings around his eyes for hours...

But anyway, no, I don't have any, you know, hard evidence. I just know what I see.
Do you believe other people, besides your husband’s sister, are also trying to harm you or take advantage of you?

Other people? No, no, it's just her. Just my husband's sister. I don't have any trouble with anyone else, really. I mean, the neighbors are fine, the people at the grocery store are fine. I go to the same cashier every Tuesday, Brenda. She's a sweetheart. She always asks about my garden. I grow tomatoes, mostly. Big, juicy beefsteaks. You have to stake them up high, though, or the vines just sprawl everywhere and the bugs get them. I use those green wooden stakes you get at the hardware store. The last time I went to get some, the kid working the register couldn't figure out the barcode scanner. He kept swiping it and swiping it, and it just kept beeping this sad little beep. It reminded me of the sound my old microwave used to make when it was finished, just before it finally died. It sparked one day, right in the middle of heating up a bowl of leftover chili. Scared me half to death. The sparks were blue, like those little sparklers we used to give the kids on the Fourth of July. You know, the ones on the wire sticks? You have to be careful with those, they get so hot. My cousin Jimmy burned a hole right through his favorite t-shirt with one when we were kids. He cried for an hour, not because he was hurt, but because it had the Dukes of Hazzard car on it... 

What was I saying? Oh, right. No, nobody else is trying to do anything to me. Just her. She's the only one causing all this trouble.
Has your husband's sister actually done anything that would be impossible in real life?

Wait, didn't you just ask me that? About impossible things? I'm pretty sure you just asked me that. No, she hasn't done anything impossible. She's just sneaky. Like I said, just regular sneaky. 

It's funny how you can ask a question twice like that and it just... echoes. My husband does that sometimes when he's watching the baseball game. He'll ask me if we have any potato chips, and I'll say no, and then five minutes later, during a commercial for car insurance or something, he'll ask again. "Did you say we have chips?" Like the first time didn't register. He loves those kettle-cooked ones, the jalapeño flavor. I can't eat them, they give me terrible heartburn. I have to take those little pink chalky pills if I even look at anything spicy. I bought a bottle of them at the pharmacy last week, and the pharmacist, Mr. Peterson, he told me he's retiring next month. Moving to Florida to live near his daughter. She just had a baby, a little girl. They named her Hazel. I think that's such an old-fashioned name, but it's coming back, isn't it? Like Evelyn and Beatrice. My grandmother's name was Beatrice. She used to make the best peach cobbler in the summertime. She'd get the peaches from this farm stand down the road...

But anyway, yeah, I already told you. Nothing impossible. Just... she's just up to no good, that's all.
Before this started with your husband’s sister, did you ever have a fixed belief like this about anyone else?

No, no, I've never thought anything like this before about anyone else. It's just her. I've always gotten along with people just fine. Well, mostly fine. There was this one time, years ago, when I thought the mailman was leaving my catalogs on the porch step instead of in the box on purpose, just so they'd get wet when it rained. But that wasn't a... a belief, really. He was just lazy. 

It rains so much here in the spring, doesn't it? The yard gets so muddy. My husband tracked mud all over the kitchen floor just yesterday. I had just mopped it, too, with that pine-scented cleaner. I love that smell. It reminds me of the Christmas trees we used to get when the kids were little. We'd drive out to this farm and cut one down ourselves. My oldest, he always wanted the biggest tree he could find, even if it wouldn't fit through the front door. We had to saw the bottom off one year right there on the porch, and sawdust got everywhere. The dog—we had a golden retriever named Buster then—he rolled in the sawdust and tracked it all over the house. Just like my husband with the mud. Buster was such a good dog, though. He lived to be fourteen. We buried him out in the backyard under the old oak tree... 

But no, to answer your question, I've never had a problem like this with anyone before. Just her.
Because of this problem, have you stopped taking care of yourself the way you usually do?

Taking care of myself? Oh, no, I haven't stopped doing any of my normal things. I still keep up with my quilting group, and choir practice, and my GED lessons. Oh, and my senior walks, I still do those like I always have. We walk around the reservoir on Wednesday mornings. You really have to watch where you step out there right now because of the geese. They leave such a mess all over the paved path. 

One of the ladies in the walking group, Martha, she actually slipped on a wet patch of leaves last fall and twisted her ankle real bad. She had to wear this big gray medical boot for six weeks. It looked so heavy, I don't know how people even drive with those things on. My uncle wore one of those when he broke his toe dropping a frozen turkey on his foot. It was Thanksgiving of... oh, it must have been 1992, I think. We had to order Chinese food that year because the turkey was completely ruined. I actually prefer Chinese food anyway, to be honest. The sweet and sour pork at the place down the street is just wonderful, and they always give you those little crispy noodles in the bag with the duck sauce. I could eat a whole bowl of just the noodles...

But, oh, I'm sorry, you were asking about my routine. Right. So no, my day-to-day is fine. Mostly, this whole situation has just changed how much I trust my husband's sister. That's the main thing. That, and it changes which family gatherings I actually feel comfortable going to now. If I know she's going to be there, I have to think twice about it.
Has your husband’s sister ever done anything clearly concrete, like changing a bank account, removing you from a business decision, or taking money?

Well, yes, that is exactly why I came in here to talk to somebody. She has been working this family business of ours just so she can get control of the money and push me completely out of the decisions. And no matter how folks try to smooth it over, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. 

They always try to smooth things over, don't they? Especially my mother-in-law. She just hates any kind of conflict. She'll just bake a pie and pretend everything is perfectly fine. She makes this pecan pie that is just... well, it's mostly corn syrup, to be honest. You eat a slice of it and your teeth just ache for hours. I actually had to go to the dentist last month because of a terrible toothache. Dr. Evans. He’s got this big beautiful aquarium in his waiting room with these little neon fish that glow in the dark. The grandkids just love watching them dart around. My youngest grandson, Tommy, he begged for a fish tank for his birthday, but his mother said absolutely not, she wasn't going to be the one cleaning the green algae out of it every week. Which is fair, I suppose. I had a goldfish when I was a little girl, won it at the county fair tossing ping pong balls into those little glass bowls. It only lived for about a week, though. We flushed it down the toilet and I cried all afternoon... 

But anyway, yes, the business decisions and the money. That is exactly what she is doing.

Well, I came because... it’s my husband’s sister. She has been working this family business, just scheming so she can get control of the money and push me right out of all the decisions. And no matter how folks try to smooth it over, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. It’s clear as day. 

Just like... well, speaking of a year, last year around this time we had that awful freeze. Do you remember that? It completely wiped out my garden. I had these big, beautiful beefsteak tomatoes growing, and I even told my neighbor she better cover hers up with a tarp or she'd lose them all. I always get my tarps from that little hardware store off Route 9, but they shut down recently. It’s a real shame, too, because the new place that opened up in town just doesn't carry the heavy-duty ones, and their parking lot is always such a mess with all the potholes. You can barely get a cart through there without twisting an ankle. 

Anyway, I just... I needed to tell someone what's going on with her.

doctor.question: Do you believe for certain that your husband’s sister is deliberately trying to take control of the money and push you out?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I came because my husband’s sister has been working this family business so she can get control of the money and push me out of decisions, and no matter how folks try to smooth it over, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I believe 'for certain' that my husband's sister is trying to take control and push me out, which directly addresses the fixed, unchangeable nature of my belief (Delusions).

patient.answer:
Well, yes, like I was just saying, I am one hundred percent certain. I've been watching her for over a year now, and no matter how much folks try to smooth it over and make excuses for her, I know she's trying to grab the money and push me out of all the decisions with the business. 

Money just... well, it makes people act so ugly. Speaking of money, I went down to the bank on Tuesday to cash a small check, and you know that teller, the one with the bright red glasses? Well, she had this new haircut, just all chopped up in the back. I don't know why anyone would pay good money for a haircut like that. My cousin Tammy went to cosmetology school back in the nineties, down in... oh, what was the name of that town? It was right past the county line, had that big water tower. Anyway, Tammy always said if you don't layer it right, you end up looking like a wet poodle. And that's exactly what this teller looked like. I almost offered her a hat, it was that bad. She took forever counting my bills, too. 

But, um... what was I saying? Oh, right, my husband's sister. Yes, I'm certain about what she's doing.

inference.note: Persistent, fixed persecutory belief for >1 year strongly supports F22/F60.0. Tangential/circumstantial speech is present, but there is still insufficient evidence for mood episode, broader schizophrenia-spectrum symptoms, or brief duration to rule in/out F31.2, F20.9, or F23, so the list remains unchanged.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed persecutory belief occurs in isolation or alongside hallucinations, which helps distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia-spectrum and mood-related psychosis.
doctor.question: Do you ever hear voices when no one else is there?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about auditory hallucinations (hearing voices), which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Voices? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. Just regular folks talking. But speaking of hearing things, I was sitting on my porch yesterday evening, and the neighbor's dog—that little scruffy terrier mix they got from the pound—would not stop barking. Just yapping and yapping at every car that went by. They let him out on a long chain, and he gets tangled around the old oak tree in their front yard. I told my husband, I said, 'If they don't untangle that poor dog, he's gonna choke himself.' 

My husband, he just tunes it out. He can sit in his recliner with the television blaring, watching those old Westerns. You know, the ones in black and white where they always have a shootout at high noon? He loves those. We had to buy a new antenna for the TV last month because the wind blew the old one right off the roof. The guy who came to fix it was so young, he looked like he should still be in high school. I offered him some lemonade, but he said he was in a hurry to get to his next job over in Shelbyville. 

But no, to answer your question, I don't hear any voices that aren't there. Just the dog and the TV, mostly.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed persecutory belief is bizarre/impossible, which helps distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis.
doctor.question: Has your husband’s sister done anything that would be impossible for most people, like controlling your thoughts or sending you special messages?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about bizarre delusions, such as thought control or special messages (which are symptoms of schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders). The symptom profile does not contain a specific item for bizarre delusions, only the primary non-bizarre delusion about the husband's sister (S019), which was already addressed.

patient.answer:
Controlling my thoughts? Lord, no. She's not a witch or anything, she can't do things like that. No special messages either. 

Though, speaking of messages, our mail carrier—Gary, I think his name is, he wears those little blue shorts even when it's freezing out—he keeps leaving the neighbor's mail in my box. Just yesterday I got a whole stack of those glossy catalogs meant for the folks two doors down. One of them was for that fancy outdoor furniture, you know the kind with the thick cushions that cost an arm and a leg? I always say, why pay that much when the squirrels are just gonna chew right through them anyway. We had a squirrel get onto our back porch last spring, just tore the stuffing right out of the seat on my favorite rocking chair. My husband tried to patch it up with silver duct tape, which looks just awful. I told him we should go down to the flea market on Sunday and see if we can find a replacement cushion, but he hates the traffic over by the fairgrounds. It does get backed up all the way to the highway when they have the antique shows. 

But, um, what were you asking me? Oh, right, his sister. No, she can't control my mind or do anything impossible. She's just a regular, sneaky person trying to get her hands on the business money, that's all.

inference.note: No hallucinations or bizarre delusions endorsed; persecutory fixed belief >1 year persists. This supports F22/F60.0 most strongly but does not yet fully exclude F31.2, F23, or F20.9 without mood, functional decline, and broader psychotic symptom assessment.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a distinct period of abnormally elevated or irritable mood suggestive of mania, which would help distinguish bipolar disorder with psychotic features from delusional or schizophrenia-spectrum disorders.
doctor.question: Have you had a period when your mood was unusually high or irritable for days at a time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about manic or hypomanic symptoms (unusually high or irritable mood for days at a time), which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Unusually high? Or irritable? No, I wouldn't say that. I'm pretty even-keeled, mostly. I mean, everybody gets a little cranky now and then, but not for days on end. 

Now, if you want to talk about irritable, you should see my husband when his truck won't start. He's got this old Ford, 1998 I think, maroon color, but the clear coat is peeling off the hood so bad it looks like the poor thing has a terrible sunburn. He just refuses to get it painted. We took it down to the mechanic a few weeks ago... Sal, I think his name is? He's got that big garage over on Elm, right next to the diner. His shop always smells like old French fries because of the exhaust fan from the kitchen next door blowing right into his open bays. 

That diner used to have the absolute best cherry pie, but they changed owners last fall. The new guy brought in all these fancy menus with those thick plastic covers, and they always stick together when it's humid out. I just can't stand that. You try to open it up to look at the breakfast specials and it makes this awful ripping sound, like you're tearing the whole thing apart. And they stopped serving the cherry pie, too. Replaced it with some kind of lemon tart that's just way too sour. I told the waitress, I said, 'Nobody wants a sour dessert after a heavy meal,' but she just smiled and gave me the check. 

But, um... wait, what was the question again? My mood? Right, right. No, I don't get high or irritable like that. I'm just my regular self.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed persecutory belief is accompanied by markedly disorganized speech, which would help distinguish schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis from delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Do people ever tell you that your speech is hard to follow or that you go off track when you talk?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about disorganized speech (derailment or incoherence), which is a symptom of Schizophrenia (Criterion A3), but this is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Hard to follow? Off track? Well, I suppose sometimes my husband says I talk too much, but he's not one to talk. He barely says two words most days unless it's about his garden. 

He planted these Big Boy tomatoes this year, right along the back fence where the sun hits best in the afternoon. But you know, the deer keep getting into them. They just hop right over the chain-link like it's nothing. I told him we need to put up some of that chicken wire, maybe string up some shiny pie tins to scare them off. My grandmother used to do that. She had this huge garden out behind her farmhouse, and she'd hang these old aluminum pie plates from the branches of her peach trees. They'd clatter together in the wind and make this awful racket. It worked, though. We used to sit out on her wraparound porch and pit peaches all afternoon for canning. She made the best peach preserves, used real cane sugar and a little pinch of nutmeg. I tried making it once, but I scorched the bottom of the pan and it took me three days of soaking to get the burnt sugar off. I ended up having to use baking soda and a wire brush, and it scratched the enamel right off my favorite Dutch oven. 

Anyway... what were you saying? Oh, my speech. No, nobody really tells me I'm hard to follow. I just like to explain things properly, you know?

doctor.intent: Determine whether her fixed persecutory belief is non-bizarre and circumscribed versus part of a broader psychotic syndrome with negative/disorganized symptoms by assessing functional deterioration.
doctor.question: Aside from the conflict with your husband’s sister, have you been having trouble managing your usual day-to-day activities?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I still keep up with my quilting group, choir practice, GED lessons, and my senior walks like I always have. Mostly this has changed how much I trust my husband's sister and which family gatherings I feel comfortable going to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have trouble managing my usual day-to-day activities aside from the conflict with my husband's sister. This directly maps to 'Additional Requirement 1', which states that functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion or its ramifications.

patient.answer:
Trouble managing my day-to-day? Oh, no, I'm doing just fine with all that. I still keep up with my quilting group on Tuesdays, and choir practice on Thursday nights. We're actually learning this beautiful new arrangement of "Amazing Grace" right now. Our choir director, Mr. Henderson, he's got this booming baritone voice, but he's so particular about the sopranos hitting their high notes. He makes us do these silly warm-up exercises where we have to buzz our lips like a horse. It looks absolutely ridiculous, let me tell you. Mrs. Gable, she sits next to me in the alto section, and she always wears this bright red lipstick that ends up smeared all over her chin by the time we're done warming up. I keep telling her she ought to switch to one of those long-lasting stains, you know, the kind you have to scrub off with cold cream. I bought a tube of it at the pharmacy last week—the one over on Main Street, not the big chain store out by the highway. The pharmacist there, Dave, he always gives me a little discount on my vitamins. He's got a son who just started high school, playing trumpet in the marching band. They had their first game on Friday, and it rained cats and dogs. Those poor kids in their wool uniforms must have smelled like wet dogs by the end of the night. 

Oh, and I'm still doing my GED lessons, and my senior walks at the mall on Monday mornings. So, no, my daily stuff is fine. Mostly, this whole thing with his sister has just changed how much I trust her, you know? And it definitely makes me think twice about which family gatherings I feel comfortable going to. I skipped the Labor Day barbecue entirely because I just couldn't stomach the thought of her being there.

inference.note: Ruled out F31.2 and F23: no manic symptoms, no hallucinations or bizarre delusions, symptoms present >1 year, preserved day-to-day functioning. Persistent non-bizarre persecutory delusion keeps F22 highest; tangential/circumstantial speech leaves F20.9 possible; suspiciousness also compatible with F60.0.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the suspicious belief is a fixed delusion with absent insight versus longstanding suspicious personality traits, helping distinguish delusional disorder from paranoid personality disorder and schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Has anyone been able to convince you that you might be mistaken about your husband’s sister?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I came because my husband’s sister has been working this family business so she can get control of the money and push me out of decisions, and no matter how folks try to smooth it over, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if anyone has been able to convince the patient that she might be mistaken about her husband's sister. This directly assesses whether the patient's belief is fixed and resistant to contradictory evidence, which corresponds to the 'Delusions' symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Mistaken? Oh, no. People try to smooth it over, sure. They say, "Oh, she's just being helpful," or "She's just trying to pitch in." But I came because my husband’s sister has been working this family business so she can get control of all the money and push me right out of any decisions. And no matter what folks say, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. 

It's just like when my cousin Larry tried to take over my uncle's hardware store. Larry was always a smooth talker, you know? He'd come in with these big boxes of donuts from that bakery downtown—the one with the pink awning that got blown off in the storm last spring. They never did replace that awning, just left the metal frame sitting there looking like an old skeleton. Anyway, Larry would bring these donuts, the glazed ones with the little sprinkles, and sit in the back office acting like he owned the place. He started ordering all this inventory nobody wanted, like those electric snow shovels. Who buys an electric snow shovel? You just end up dragging a cord through the wet snow, and then you trip over it and break your hip. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she broke her hip two winters ago slipping on the ice by her mailbox. She was in rehab for months, and when she came back, she had to use one of those walkers with the tennis balls on the feet. I always wondered who came up with that idea, putting tennis balls on walkers. It seems so silly, but I guess it stops them from scuffing up the linoleum. 

But, what was I... oh, right. No, I'm not mistaken. She's trying to push me out, and nobody can convince me otherwise. I see right through her.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the suspicious belief is confined to this single theme or part of a broader longstanding pattern of distrust, helping distinguish delusional disorder from paranoid personality disorder and schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Before all this with your husband’s sister, have you generally found it hard to trust other people?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a general or historical difficulty trusting other people, which relates to paranoid personality traits or general paranoia, but the provided symptom profile only covers the specific delusion regarding the husband's sister (S019), functioning (additional_requirement_1, functional_impairment), and duration.

patient.answer:
Hard to trust people? No, not really. I've always been a pretty trusting person, you know? I mean, I try to see the good in folks. Like my neighbor down the street, Mr. Abernathy. 

He moved in about three years ago, right after his wife passed away. She had a bad heart, I think. Anyway, he started leaving these little baskets of vegetables from his garden on my front porch. Just out of the blue! Zucchini, mostly. You know how zucchini is, once it starts growing, you can't stop it. You have to practically give it away to strangers on the street. I made so much zucchini bread that summer, I thought my husband was going to turn green. I use my mother's recipe, the one with the walnuts and a little bit of cinnamon. But walnuts are getting so expensive these days. I was at the grocery store last week—the one with the new self-checkout lanes that never seem to work right—and a little bag of walnuts was almost eight dollars! Can you believe that? The cashier, a sweet young girl named Chloe, she said it's because of a drought somewhere out west. She's saving up for college, wants to study marine biology. I always thought that sounded so interesting, working with dolphins and whales. I saw a documentary once about these whales that sing to each other across the ocean. It's so beautiful, but a little sad, too, don't you think? Just calling out into the dark water, hoping someone hears you. 

But, um... what were we talking about? Oh, trusting people. No, before this whole mess with her, I never really had a problem trusting people. I just take them as they come.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed persecutory belief is based on real evidence or is implausible/delusional, to distinguish delusional disorder from paranoid personality traits and schizophrenia.
doctor.question: What exactly has your husband’s sister done that makes you believe she is trying to take control of the money and push you out?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for specific details or evidence about what the sister-in-law has done to make the patient believe she is trying to take control of the money. None of the symptom profiles provide specific examples of the sister's actions, only the general belief (Delusions), its impact on functioning (Additional Requirement 1 / Functional Impairment), and its duration.

patient.answer:
Well, it's just... it's the way she acts, you know? She's always hovering around the business accounts, always asking these little questions about where the money's going. And she started bringing in these fancy new ledger books. I don't know what was wrong with the old ones, the green ones with the gold lettering on the front. We used to buy them at that stationery shop downtown, the one next to the old movie theater. 

They tore that theater down last year, you know. It was a shame, really. I saw my first movie there, "The Sound of Music." My mother took me, and we sat right in the middle row. The seats were covered in this red velvet that was practically worn bald on the armrests. And they had the best popcorn. They used real butter, not that yellow oil stuff they squirt on it now. My husband loves popcorn, but he always burns it in the microwave. He sets the timer for three minutes and then walks away to watch the news. The news is just so depressing lately, isn't it? All these storms and things. My sister-in-law in Florida—not the one I'm talking about, my brother's wife—she had to evacuate twice last year because of hurricanes. She packed up her two cats and drove all the way up to Georgia. The cats hated it, of course. One of them, a big orange tabby named Marmalade, yowled the entire six hours. I had an orange cat once, when I was a little girl... 

But I'm sorry, what did you ask me? What exactly did she do? Well, I don't know exactly, it's just... I just know she's trying to push me out. You can just tell with some people, can't you?

doctor.intent: Determine whether the belief about the sister-in-law is a fixed delusion based on minimal evidence versus a personality-based suspiciousness or broader psychotic disorder, by testing conviction despite lack of concrete proof.
doctor.question: Is it possible that you could be wrong about your husband’s sister?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I came because my husband’s sister has been working this family business so she can get control of the money and push me out of decisions, and no matter how folks try to smooth it over, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is again asking if the patient could be wrong about her husband's sister, which directly probes the fixity of her belief (Delusions).

patient.answer:
Wrong? No, no, I couldn't be wrong. Like I said before, I came here because my husband's sister has been working this family business just so she can get control of the money and push me out of all the decisions. People try to smooth it over, tell me I'm imagining things, but no matter what folks try to say, I know what I've been seeing for more than a year now. 

It's just like when you see a storm rolling in. You know it's coming. The sky gets that weird greenish-purple color, like a bruised plum. My grandmother used to make the best plum preserves. She had this big copper pot she'd stir them in, and she'd stand over the stove for hours with this long wooden spoon. The spoon was stained dark purple at the end. She always said the secret was a pinch of nutmeg, but I think it was just the amount of sugar she used. She kept her sugar in this old tin canister that had a picture of a windmill on it. I always liked that windmill. I wanted to visit Holland when I was younger, to see the tulips and the windmills. I saw a picture in a magazine once of a whole field of red and yellow tulips. It looked like a quilt spread out over the ground. My aunt made me a quilt for my wedding, actually. It was a double wedding ring pattern, all done in blues and whites. But the dog we had then—a little terrier mix named Buster—he chewed a hole right through the corner of it. He was a good dog, though, just a little anxious during thunderstorms... 

But anyway, no, I'm not wrong about her. I've been watching her for a year, and I know exactly what she's trying to do with the business and the money. I see it plain as day.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed persecutory belief is bizarre or non-bizarre, which best separates delusional disorder from schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Has your husband's sister done anything that would be impossible in real life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the husband's sister has done anything impossible in real life (checking for bizarre delusions), which is not covered in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Impossible? Like magic or something? No, she hasn't done anything like that. She's just sneaky, you know? Just... regular sneaky. Although, I swear sometimes it feels like she can read my mind, the way she knows exactly when I'm going to check the mail so she can get to the bank statements first. Our mail carrier, Gary, he's been doing this route for twenty years. He walks with a little bit of a limp now because he slipped on the ice on Mrs. Higgins' driveway two winters ago. She never shovels her walk, Mrs. Higgins. She just throws down this cheap rock salt that ruins the concrete. It eats right through it, leaves these little pockmarks everywhere. My husband tried to tell her once, but she just waved him off. She's practically deaf in one ear, anyway. She used to play the French horn in the symphony orchestra, back in the sixties. I can't imagine carrying one of those big brass things around, they look so heavy and complicated. All those valves and tubes. My nephew played the trumpet in middle school, but he gave it up because it made his lips swell up...

Wait, what did you ask me? Impossible things? No, no, nothing impossible. Just... very underhanded.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's fixed persecutory belief is non-bizarre and isolated rather than part of broader schizophrenia-spectrum symptoms, by assessing whether the belief is based on concrete evidence.
doctor.question: What specific evidence do you have that makes you sure your husband’s sister is trying to take control of the money?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for specific evidence supporting the delusion. While the delusion itself is covered under S019, the specific evidence is not detailed in the symptom profile, and S019 was already used.

patient.answer:
Evidence? Well, I don't... I don't have, like, a piece of paper or a recording or anything like that. It's just... I just know it. It's the way she looks at the ledgers, the way she asks about the accounts. You don't need a photograph to know someone's sneaking around behind your back. 

My mother used to say that, actually. She'd say, "You don't need a weatherman to know which way the wind blows." She loved that song, the Bob Dylan one. We had it on an old 45 record. The label was yellow and orange, I think. We kept all the records in this wooden crate in the living room, right next to the console television. That TV was a piece of furniture, I tell you. It had these big wooden doors you could close over the screen when you weren't watching it. Not like these flat things people hang on the wall now. They just look like black mirrors when they're turned off. I don't like them. They reflect everything in the room. I saw myself in one at the appliance store the other day and I thought, "Lord, when did I get so gray?" My hairdresser, Patty, she says she can put a rinse in it, but I don't know. Those chemicals smell so strong. They remind me of the pool at the YMCA where my kids took swimming lessons. The chlorine was so thick you could taste it in the air. My youngest, he hated getting his face wet. He'd wear these little goggles that left red rings around his eyes for hours...

But anyway, no, I don't have any, you know, hard evidence. I just know what I see.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a fixed non-bizarre delusion from a longstanding paranoid personality pattern by determining whether this suspicious belief is confined to the sister-in-law/business situation or extends to other people.
doctor.question: Do you believe other people, besides your husband’s sister, are also trying to harm you or take advantage of you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient believes other people besides her husband's sister are trying to harm or take advantage of her (checking for other persecutory delusions). The provided symptom profiles only cover the delusions about the husband's sister (S019), functional impairment, and duration, but do not contain a specific item addressing whether the patient has delusions about *other* people.

patient.answer:
Other people? No, no, it's just her. Just my husband's sister. I don't have any trouble with anyone else, really. I mean, the neighbors are fine, the people at the grocery store are fine. I go to the same cashier every Tuesday, Brenda. She's a sweetheart. She always asks about my garden. I grow tomatoes, mostly. Big, juicy beefsteaks. You have to stake them up high, though, or the vines just sprawl everywhere and the bugs get them. I use those green wooden stakes you get at the hardware store. The last time I went to get some, the kid working the register couldn't figure out the barcode scanner. He kept swiping it and swiping it, and it just kept beeping this sad little beep. It reminded me of the sound my old microwave used to make when it was finished, just before it finally died. It sparked one day, right in the middle of heating up a bowl of leftover chili. Scared me half to death. The sparks were blue, like those little sparklers we used to give the kids on the Fourth of July. You know, the ones on the wire sticks? You have to be careful with those, they get so hot. My cousin Jimmy burned a hole right through his favorite t-shirt with one when we were kids. He cried for an hour, not because he was hurt, but because it had the Dukes of Hazzard car on it... 

What was I saying? Oh, right. No, nobody else is trying to do anything to me. Just her. She's the only one causing all this trouble.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed persecutory belief is bizarre/impossible or non-bizarre/plausible, which best separates delusional disorder from schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis.
doctor.question: Has your husband's sister actually done anything that would be impossible in real life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the husband's sister has done anything impossible in real life, which is a question aimed at determining if the delusions are bizarre or non-bizarre. The symptom profiles provide information about the presence of delusions (S019), functional impairment, and duration, but none specifically address the bizarre/non-bizarre nature of the delusions (e.g., whether the events are physically possible).

patient.answer:
Wait, didn't you just ask me that? About impossible things? I'm pretty sure you just asked me that. No, she hasn't done anything impossible. She's just sneaky. Like I said, just regular sneaky. 

It's funny how you can ask a question twice like that and it just... echoes. My husband does that sometimes when he's watching the baseball game. He'll ask me if we have any potato chips, and I'll say no, and then five minutes later, during a commercial for car insurance or something, he'll ask again. "Did you say we have chips?" Like the first time didn't register. He loves those kettle-cooked ones, the jalapeño flavor. I can't eat them, they give me terrible heartburn. I have to take those little pink chalky pills if I even look at anything spicy. I bought a bottle of them at the pharmacy last week, and the pharmacist, Mr. Peterson, he told me he's retiring next month. Moving to Florida to live near his daughter. She just had a baby, a little girl. They named her Hazel. I think that's such an old-fashioned name, but it's coming back, isn't it? Like Evelyn and Beatrice. My grandmother's name was Beatrice. She used to make the best peach cobbler in the summertime. She'd get the peaches from this farm stand down the road...

But anyway, yeah, I already told you. Nothing impossible. Just... she's just up to no good, that's all.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed belief is a circumscribed non-bizarre delusion without broader negative symptoms or personality baseline suspiciousness, favoring delusional disorder over schizophrenia or paranoid personality disorder.
doctor.question: Before this started with your husband’s sister, did you ever have a fixed belief like this about anyone else?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient has ever had similar fixed beliefs about anyone else prior to this situation with her husband's sister, which assesses past history of delusions. This is not covered by the current symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no, I've never thought anything like this before about anyone else. It's just her. I've always gotten along with people just fine. Well, mostly fine. There was this one time, years ago, when I thought the mailman was leaving my catalogs on the porch step instead of in the box on purpose, just so they'd get wet when it rained. But that wasn't a... a belief, really. He was just lazy. 

It rains so much here in the spring, doesn't it? The yard gets so muddy. My husband tracked mud all over the kitchen floor just yesterday. I had just mopped it, too, with that pine-scented cleaner. I love that smell. It reminds me of the Christmas trees we used to get when the kids were little. We'd drive out to this farm and cut one down ourselves. My oldest, he always wanted the biggest tree he could find, even if it wouldn't fit through the front door. We had to saw the bottom off one year right there on the porch, and sawdust got everywhere. The dog—we had a golden retriever named Buster then—he rolled in the sawdust and tracked it all over the house. Just like my husband with the mud. Buster was such a good dog, though. He lived to be fourteen. We buried him out in the backyard under the old oak tree... 

But no, to answer your question, I've never had a problem like this with anyone before. Just her.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a marked decline in functioning or self-care suggestive of schizophrenia rather than a circumscribed delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Because of this problem, have you stopped taking care of yourself the way you usually do?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I still keep up with my quilting group, choir practice, GED lessons, and my senior walks like I always have. Mostly this has changed how much I trust my husband's sister and which family gatherings I feel comfortable going to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient has stopped taking care of themselves the way they usually do, which relates to whether their functioning is markedly impaired. The 'Additional Requirement 1' item covers how their functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion, and mentions keeping up with usual routines like quilting, choir, GED lessons, and senior walks.

patient.answer:
Taking care of myself? Oh, no, I haven't stopped doing any of my normal things. I still keep up with my quilting group, and choir practice, and my GED lessons. Oh, and my senior walks, I still do those like I always have. We walk around the reservoir on Wednesday mornings. You really have to watch where you step out there right now because of the geese. They leave such a mess all over the paved path. 

One of the ladies in the walking group, Martha, she actually slipped on a wet patch of leaves last fall and twisted her ankle real bad. She had to wear this big gray medical boot for six weeks. It looked so heavy, I don't know how people even drive with those things on. My uncle wore one of those when he broke his toe dropping a frozen turkey on his foot. It was Thanksgiving of... oh, it must have been 1992, I think. We had to order Chinese food that year because the turkey was completely ruined. I actually prefer Chinese food anyway, to be honest. The sweet and sour pork at the place down the street is just wonderful, and they always give you those little crispy noodles in the bag with the duck sauce. I could eat a whole bowl of just the noodles...

But, oh, I'm sorry, you were asking about my routine. Right. So no, my day-to-day is fine. Mostly, this whole situation has just changed how much I trust my husband's sister. That's the main thing. That, and it changes which family gatherings I actually feel comfortable going to now. If I know she's going to be there, I have to think twice about it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed belief is based on a non-bizarre, plausible situation versus bizarre psychotic content, to distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia-spectrum illness.
doctor.question: Has your husband’s sister ever done anything clearly concrete, like changing a bank account, removing you from a business decision, or taking money?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I came because my husband’s sister has been working this family business so she can get control of the money and push me out of decisions, and no matter how folks try to smooth it over, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for concrete evidence of the sister-in-law's actions (changing bank accounts, removing the patient from decisions, taking money), which relates to the manifestation of the patient's delusion that the sister-in-law is trying to get control of the money and push her out of decisions.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, that is exactly why I came in here to talk to somebody. She has been working this family business of ours just so she can get control of the money and push me completely out of the decisions. And no matter how folks try to smooth it over, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. 

They always try to smooth things over, don't they? Especially my mother-in-law. She just hates any kind of conflict. She'll just bake a pie and pretend everything is perfectly fine. She makes this pecan pie that is just... well, it's mostly corn syrup, to be honest. You eat a slice of it and your teeth just ache for hours. I actually had to go to the dentist last month because of a terrible toothache. Dr. Evans. He’s got this big beautiful aquarium in his waiting room with these little neon fish that glow in the dark. The grandkids just love watching them dart around. My youngest grandson, Tommy, he begged for a fish tank for his birthday, but his mother said absolutely not, she wasn't going to be the one cleaning the green algae out of it every week. Which is fair, I suppose. I had a goldfish when I was a little girl, won it at the county fair tossing ping pong balls into those little glass bowls. It only lived for about a week, though. We flushed it down the toilet and I cried all afternoon... 

But anyway, yes, the business decisions and the money. That is exactly what she is doing.

opening_question.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a single, persistent, non-bizarre persecutory belief focused on her husband's sister trying to control business money and exclude her, held with delusional conviction for more than a year despite lack of evidence and failed reassurance. She denies hallucinations, thought control, special messages, and sustained mood episodes, and there is no broader pattern of psychotic symptoms or deterioration suggestive of schizophrenia. Longstanding pervasive suspiciousness predating this issue is also denied, arguing against paranoid personality disorder.
